project.topic: An agentic, rubric-aware system that turns a rough research idea into a complete, citation-grounded research proposal through human-in-the-loop critique and a verifiable revision loop
project.title: Rubric-Aware Agentic Proposal Builder with Human-in-the-Loop Critique and Verifiable Revision
project.keywords: research proposal generation, agentic AI, rubric-aware evaluation, human-in-the-loop revision, citation grounding, verifiable LLM systems
project.abstract: This project proposes an agentic, rubric-aware system that helps researchers transform a rough research idea into a complete, citation-grounded research proposal. The system decomposes proposal writing into specialized stages: requirement extraction, section planning, literature and source grounding, draft generation, rubric-based critique, human feedback incorporation, and verifiable revision. Unlike generic large language model writing assistants, the proposed system explicitly represents proposal requirements as a checklist and uses iterative critique loops to detect missing sections, unsupported claims, weak novelty statements, and evaluation gaps. A human-in-the-loop interface allows users to accept, reject, or modify agent suggestions while preserving an auditable revision history. The expected outcome is a prototype that improves proposal completeness, alignment with rubrics, citation traceability, and user efficiency compared with baseline LLM drafting workflows.
project.problem: Researchers need structured, rubric-compliant, citation-grounded proposals, but generic LLM assistants often omit requirements, hallucinate citations, and provide limited auditable revision support.
project.novelty: The system differs from generic writing assistants, retrieval-augmented chatbots, and automated critique tools by treating the proposal rubric as an executable specification and linking each revision to checklist items, source evidence, and user decisions.
project.goal: The goal is to design, implement, and evaluate a prototype system that converts a rough research idea into a complete research proposal while improving rubric coverage, citation grounding, revision transparency, and user control compared with a single-pass LLM drafting baseline.
project.method: Use intake, planning, retrieval, drafting, rubric critique, human decision, and revision agents operating over a structured JSON proposal state and audit log.
project.figure: Show a pipeline from user idea and rubric to requirement extraction, planning, retrieval, drafting, critique, human decisions, revision, and final proposal, with feedback loops and an evidence store.
project.expectedResults: Expected results include: (1) a working prototype that accepts a rough research idea and checklist and outputs a structured proposal; (2) a rubric-to-section mapping that shows which requirements are satisfied; (3) citation-grounded claims with source metadata or source notes; (4) an iterative critique and revision mechanism that improves proposal quality over multiple turns; and (5) an evaluation report comparing the system against baseline LLM drafting. Research milestones include requirements analysis, workflow design, prototype implementation, retrieval and citation grounding integration, rubric critic development, user interface development, evaluation, and final documentation.
project.timeline: Estimated 12-week timeline: Weeks 1–2: define proposal rubric, target users, evaluation criteria, and baseline workflows. Weeks 3–4: design system architecture, JSON project state, agent roles, and prompt templates. Weeks 5–6: implement intake, planning, drafting, and structured output generation. Weeks 7–8: integrate retrieval, citation metadata, and claim-source linking. Weeks 9–10: implement rubric critique, revision loop, and human decision interface. Week 11: run evaluation using sample rough ideas and human or expert ratings. Week 12: analyze results, document limitations, prepare final proposal, prototype demo, and release plan.
project.evaluation: Evaluate on 12 rough ideas across 3 domains. Metrics: required-section coverage (target 13/13), number of high-severity unsupported claims (target 0 after one revision), and a 1-5 human rubric score for novelty/method/evaluation (target mean >= 4). Compare draft v1 vs revised v2 (before/after) and against a single-shot ChatGPT baseline.
project.risks: Key risks include hallucinated or weak citations, overreliance on LLM-generated claims, poor retrieval quality, excessive workflow complexity, user fatigue from too many questions, and difficulty evaluating proposal quality objectively. Mitigations include using retrieval-grounded generation, requiring source metadata for factual claims, flagging unsupported claims, limiting open-ended questions to high-value missing information, maintaining an auditable revision log, comparing against clear baselines, and using both automatic rubric checks and human ratings.
project.resources: Required resources include access to an LLM API or open-source language model, a retrieval source such as Semantic Scholar, Crossref, OpenAlex, arXiv, institutional databases, or a curated paper corpus, a vector database or document index, a web or notebook interface, structured JSON storage for project state, and evaluation participants or expert reviewers. The release plan should include a prototype demo, prompt and workflow templates, anonymized evaluation examples, documentation, and, where licensing allows, open-source code for the agent orchestration and rubric validation components.
